lesson.title: Unpacking: Handing Tuple Values Back to Names
lesson.summary: Unpacking reverses packing: it takes a tuple's values and assigns them to separate variable names in a single statement, including a starred variable that can scoop up the leftovers.
lesson.body:
Tuple Packing bundles several values into one tuple. Unpacking does the opposite: it takes an existing tuple and spreads its values out across several variable names in a single assignment statement. This is the same Multiple Assignment mechanic you have already used to write something like a, b = 1, 2 in one line; what you may not have realized is that statement is doing two things at once, packing 1, 2 into a temporary tuple on the right, then immediately unpacking that tuple into a and b on the left.

point = (3, 4, 5)
x, y, z = point
print(x, y, z)

This prints 3 4 5. Python matched each name on the left to the value at the same position in the tuple on the right, which only works because there are exactly three names for exactly three values. If the counts do not match, Python refuses rather than guessing.

try:
    p, q = point
except ValueError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

This prints Error: too many values to unpack (expected 2, got 3), since point has three values but only two names were given to catch them.

Sometimes you genuinely do not know how many extra values there will be, and you only care about the first one or two. A starred name lets you gather everything left over into a list, instead of forcing you to name every single position.

first, *rest = point
print(first, rest)

This prints 3 [4, 5]. first grabbed the single value 3, and *rest scooped up every remaining value into a list, even though the tuple itself is not a list. Unpacking also gives you the classic one-line variable swap, which works because the right-hand side is packed into a temporary tuple using the old values before either name on the left is touched.

a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

This prints 20 10. Python evaluates b, a first, using the original values 20 and 10, packs them into a tuple, and only then unpacks that tuple into a and b, which is why no temporary variable is needed to perform the swap.
